claims.text: The nanoparticles have an equimolar CoCrFeMnNi composition, corresponding to approximately 20 at.% of each element.
CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles can be synthesized by ultrafast or ultrashort-pulsed laser ablation.
The as-synthesized CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles have a uniform elemental distribution.
A moderate post-synthesis anneal below the bulk melting temperature selectively segregates elements to the nanoparticle surface.
The controlled comparison is performed by in-situ TEM heating under an inert atmosphere at approximately 0.7–0.9 times the bulk melting temperature.
The anneal produces surface chemical heterogeneities through preferential segregation of lower-cohesion elements.
Surface segregation locally reduces atomic cohesive energies.
Reduced local cohesive energy initiates premelting at the nanoparticle surface.
The mobility initiated by surface premelting propagates inward through the nanoparticle.
Inward propagation of premelting mobility lowers the nanoparticle's overall melting temperature.
Annealed, surface-segregated nanoparticles will begin surface premelting at a lower temperature than unannealed, uniformly mixed nanoparticles.
Annealed, surface-segregated nanoparticles will have a lower overall melting temperature than the unannealed baseline.
The predicted annealing effect will be consistently observable for particles between 5 and 20 nm.
The baseline consists of unannealed CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles without deliberately induced surface segregation.
The unannealed baseline maintains higher surface cohesive energies than the annealed, segregated particles.
Higher surface cohesive energies cause the baseline particles to premelt later and melt at a higher temperature.
The hypothesis is bounded to 5–20 nm CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles under an inert atmosphere.
Significant bulk compositional changes or morphological coarsening caused by annealing could alter the melting behavior and invalidate the proposed range of applicability.
Thermal treatment may introduce phase, morphological, or compositional changes beyond surface segregation that could confound the melting comparison.
